summary: Ecclesiastes 6 (12 verses) continues the story of vanity. Starting with 'There is an evil which I have seen under the sun, and it is heavy on men:', it moves through themes of vanity, time and calls readers toward fear God.
whyItMatters: This chapter matters because it shows vanity lived out in jerusalem reflections. For a first-time reader, it answers: who is God in this moment, what does he ask, and how do people respond.

keyVerses.text: There is an evil which I have seen under the sun, and it is heavy on men:
All the labor of man is for his mouth, and yet the appetite is not filled.
For who knows what is good for man in life, all the days of his vain life which he spends like a shadow? For who can tell a man what will be after him under the sun?

questions.question: What is happening in Ecclesiastes 6?
questions.answer: In 12 verses, this chapter ecclesiastes 6 (12 verses) continues the story of vanity. starting with 'there is an evil which i have seen under the sun, and it is heavy on men:', it moves through themes of vanity, time and calls readers toward fear god. The setting is jerusalem reflections, written to seekers. Look for who speaks, who listens, and what changes by the end.

questions.question: Who wrote Ecclesiastes and why 6 matters in the bigger story?
questions.answer: Traditionally qoheleth, solomon tradition, addressed to seekers around ~900 bc debate. This chapter fits the book's purpose as philosophical wisdom — its themes of vanity, time build on what came before.

questions.question: Are there any difficult words here?
questions.answer: Scan for names, places, or repeated abstract words like righteousness, covenant, or glory. The glossary below defines up to 3 that show up most. Ask: who is this person, what does this word mean in everyday terms?

questions.question: What does this chapter teach about God or people?
questions.answer: Through vanity and time, it shows God's character (faithful, just, merciful) and human tendency (need, failure, hope). Notice how verses move from problem to provision.

questions.question: Verse 2 is long — what is it saying in plain English?
questions.answer: The verse says: 'a man to whom God gives riches, wealth, and honor, so that he lacks nothing for his soul of all that he desires, yet God gives him no power to eat of it, but an alien eats it. This...' In plain terms: it is making a key point about vanity. Break it into two halves — what is described, and what is promised or commanded.

questions.question: How could this chapter apply today without forcing modern ideas onto it?
questions.answer: Ask: what was original audience supposed to do with this? Then ask: what similar situation exists today? For example, if chapter warns about idols, today that might be money or status; if it celebrates deliverance, where do people need deliverance today?
